items.title: Joe Temperley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997
items.q: I don’t know if I could tackle that because it took John Coltrane two years to learn how to play that.

ctx.x: That’s a good one, yeah. You’d better do “Giant Steps” on your next record to show him how it’s done.
Oh, yeah. I don’t know if I could tackle that because it took John Coltrane two years to learn how to play that. You don’t just do that in five minutes.
Well I’ve enjoyed talking with you today.

items.title: Joe Temperley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997
items.q: I think, for instance, I think all the young, the supposed young lions, they should be playing with each other... When things were at the height, you know, the Miles Davis Sextet and the Miles Davis Quintet, it was Miles Davis and Coltrane...

ctx.x: What’s your outlook on the state of jazz these days?

Well it’s kind of fragmented, the jazz situation. And I think, for instance, I think all the young, the supposed young lions, they should be playing with each other, instead of all having their own bands. When things were at the height, you know, the Miles Davis Sextet and the Miles Davis Quintet, it was Miles Davis and Coltrane, and Philly Joe and Red Garland and Paul Chambers. But nowadays, every one of those people would have their own band. And I don’t think that’s really a good thing. I think all these young…
Well blues has got to be a part of the jazz music. And I was interested in hearing the second set last night, that they opened up with a blues tune. And it was really nice, just to hear some wailing.
